title: Influence of thymectomy on the course of myasthenia gravis and the role of the surgical procedure
summary:
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a rare disease that leads to impaired signal transmission from the nerve to the muscles. This classically results in muscle weakness due to exertion, which often manifests itself at the beginning in the area of the eye muscles with a drooping eyelid or double vision. In some patients, it can also spread (“generalize”), i.e. the muscle weakness spreads to the rest of the body, which can then lead to swallowing and chewing disorders as well as weakness of the respiratory and skeletal muscles. 
The cause of this disease is the formation of so-called autoantibodies against a protein molecule that is crucial for the transmission of signals at the neuromuscular synapse. We know that an incorrectly regulated immune system is responsible for this, as these autoantibodies are not detectable in healthy people. As a result, the immune system of MG patients, which is normally designed to combat foreign viruses or bacteria, attacks the body's own structures. 

The thymus (thymus gland) is an organ of the immune system located in the upper middle part of the chest (behind the breastbone). It is used for the maturation and differentiation of T lymphocytes - a type of white blood cell that plays an important role in the aforementioned defective regulation of the immune system. Long before the autoimmune nature of MG was recognized, studies at the beginning of the 19th century showed a connection between MG disease and tumours of the thymus gland. In fact, in 10-15% of all MG patients, a tumor of the thymus gland (thymoma), which requires surgical removal, can be detected. Many patients show a significant improvement in their myasthenic symptoms after this tumor removal. In turn, up to 70% of younger patients (onset of the disease between the ages of 15 and 50) do not have a tumor, but show a typical change in the thymus - so-called lymphofollicular hyperplasia. This is an expression of an active immunological process. Thanks to a large study, the results of which were published in 2016, it was possible to prove that surgical removal of the thymus gland also leads to an improvement in myasthenic symptoms in MG patients without a tumor (MGTX study). This leads to the conclusion that MG patients should also be treated surgically in addition to drug therapy.
In terms of surgical treatment, there are various surgical techniques for removing the thymus gland. In the past, an open thymectomy, in which the sternum is cut along its longitudinal axis, was performed. Today, gentle minimally invasive techniques (“thoracoscopic”) are increasingly being used to completely remove the thymus gland or, if necessary, its tumors. In thoracoscopy, the surgical procedure is not performed under direct vision and openly, but with the aid of an observation tube (thoracoscope). Increasingly, procedures with robotic assistance are also being used. While minimally invasive procedures are superior to open surgical procedures in terms of tolerability, it has not yet been sufficiently clarified whether the procedures are equivalent in terms of their effect on myasthenia gravis and their safety, or whether one of the procedures is better. With the present study, we want to contribute to answering this question better.
In contrast, a study was recently published which suggests that there is a higher probability of dying and developing cancer or autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatism, after a thymectomy. We also want to try to answer this important question with this study. 
We would therefore like to examine three groups of participants. Firstly, MG patients who have undergone a minimally invasive thymectomy (Tmin group) will be included in the study. On the other hand, MG patients who have undergone an open thymectomy (Toffen group) will be examined as part of the study. Their data on the disease and treatment (in particular the thymectomy performed) will then be compared with data from MG patients who have not undergone a thymectomy (T0 group). This comparison may provide information on the long-term effects of thymectomy on health.

interventions.name: Tmin: MG patients who underwent minimally invasive thymectomy
Toffen: MG patients who underwent an open thymectomy
T0: MG patients who did not undergo a thymectomy

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Confirmed diagnosis of MG
- Capacity to consent and written informed consent of the patient 
- Minimally invasive thymectomy performed ≥ 90 days ago (Tmin group) or open thymectomy ≥ 90 (Toffen group) 
OR
- No thymectomy (T0 group)
Exclusion criteria:
- Lack of communication skills
